newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalan army officers seek amnesty for murder.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan army officers seek amnesty for murder.

text.p: Three high-ranking Guatemalan army officers accused of ordering the 1990 assassination of sociologist Myrna Mack sought amnesty on Monday under the terms of a new peace treaty.

Mack, a Guatemalan, was fatally stabbed by an army soldier in a killing that sparked outrage from human rights activists, who said her ground-breaking work on the country's Indians displaced by the civil war had angered the army.

General Edgar Augusto Godoy and Colonels Juan Valencia Osorio and Juan Guillermo Oliva filed for the amnesty under a controversial part of the recent treaty ending three decades of civil war between the government and leftist rebels.
"We believe this is a political crime that falls within the (amnesty) law. The accusing party even recognised that at one point," Mario Morales, lawyer for the three army officers, told reporters.
Morales said his clients were not recognising guilt by appealing for an amnesty.
The Mack case became a landmark in Guatemala when soldier Noel de Jesus Beteta got 30 years for the crime -- the first time a member of the armed forces was convicted in a human rights case.
Godoy, Valencia and Oliva were accused earlier this year of ordering Beteta to kill Mack -- a case currently in the courts.
The move to apply for amnesty by the three army officers sparked angry reaction in a country where brutal human rights abuses marked much of the war.
Myrna Mack's sister Helen said she had anticipated the accused killers would try to take advantage of the law.
"Myrna had nothing to do with the armed conflict. She was not a subversive or a militant. She was a civilian who was assassinated. This case does not fit under the law," Helen Mack told Reuters.

Under the Dec 29 peace treaty between the government and leftist Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) rebels, the list of political crimes to receive amnesty includes sedition and rebellion, but not murder.
"This law was written in a hurry," Morales said in explaining why he was asking for amnesty for his clients for a crime not covered by the law.
At the time of her death, the government refused to recognise that hundreds of thousands of Guatemalans had been displaced by its efforts to quell the rebellion.
